Each color in the source palette carries information about the solve path. Bright saturated sources tend to appear when the target leans toward primary or secondary hues. Muted or pastel sources suggest the target sits closer to gray or has balanced channel values.

Look at the hint widget if one exists on today's page. Some versions of Colorfle include a "closest match" indicator that flags which of your three guesses is nearest to the target. That single data point can save multiple failed submissions by narrowing your search to the two weaker matches.

The solver link available on this site lets you input your current best guesses and receive feedback on channel-by-channel distance. Using that tool systematically beats random tweaking because it quantifies your errors instead of relying on eyeballing.

Why additive color logic beats random mixing

Additive color mixing follows predictable math. Red (255, 0, 0) plus Green (0, 255, 0) equals Yellow (255, 255, 0). Adding Blue (0, 0, 255) gets you to White (255, 255, 255). This isn't intuitive if you learned color theory through art class, where red plus green makes brown.

The mental shift matters. Think in terms of adding light channels together rather than blending physical pigments. When you see a target color like teal (0, 128, 128), your brain might instinctively reach for blue-green paint mixing. But digitally, teal is simply half-intensity green combined with half-intensity blue, with red set to zero.

A careful player usually notices that targets with high saturation require source colors near the corners of the RGB cube—pure or near-pure primaries and secondaries. Desaturated targets demand lower values across all three channels or careful balance toward neutral gray.

Before guessing randomly, map out the RGB cube mentally. Identify which corner of the color space your target occupies. Then work backward to determine which three sources could converge there.

If you're consistently missing by a small margin on one channel, check whether you've been underestimating how much that channel contributes to the final mix. Sometimes a color looks predominantly blue but actually contains significant green—the eye plays tricks, but the numbers don't lie.

The archive history linked from this page offers pattern recognition over multiple puzzles. Reviewing past solutions builds intuition for how often certain channel combinations appear and which color families prove trickiest.

No. The game mixes all three sources simultaneously regardless of sequence. What matters is getting each individual channel value close enough to the target that the combined result matches within the acceptable tolerance.

Zero progress typically means that particular source is completely wrong—not just slightly off. Revisit your assumption about that channel's contribution to the target. Try solving manually first for two or three puzzles, then verify with the solver to confirm your reasoning.

Gray targets require low values across all three channels with minimal variation between them. Your three sources should cluster near (128, 128, 128) or whatever gray level the target specifies. Any single channel that spikes above the others will drag the mix toward that hue.
